In previous sessions I have referred to the unfairness of the federal tax on electricity. The tax is on the cost to users of electricity generated by private enterprise and my county of Cumberland pays about $150,000 a year, while Montreal and other places served by government generated electricity and low cost financing escape paying such taxes. Heavy corporation taxes increase our costs on privately generated electric energy, but not on government hydro electricity. The tax is on the cost to users, not on the kilowatts, so that users
The Budget-Mr. P. C. Black

from the smaller and less efficient plants pay the heavy taxes. Nova Scotia built 218-5 miles of rural electrification last year, subsidized and encouraged its construction in an effort to bring modern conveniences to rural communities; and the federal government makes no contribution, assumes no responsibility, but lays on heavy electric taxes under the guise of war. Nova Scotia has a programme to build 500 miles of rural electrification next year and the following years, and Ottawa will gather in more taxes from us.
I join with the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) in his protest against Ottawa's treatment of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick with respect to the marketing of birch affected by "dieback". This affects hundreds of millions of feet of hardwood in these provinces. I resent the insinuation of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) that lumbermen of the maritime provinces cannot be trusted. We have a well established lands and forests department in Nova Scotia, now presided over by Hon. J. H. MacQuarrie, who stated in Halifax on May 10:
People at Ottawa do not know what they are doing. Ottawa was to blame for the fact that Nova Scotia lumbermen could not market birch affected by dieback, wood that would be useless in five years or less . . . We have not ceased one iota in our efforts and we will continue our efforts until we do get relief for the people of Nova Scotia. They (Ottawa) do not seem to have the faintest knowledge of the situation.
This is one more proof that Nova Scotia's interests get little consideration at Ottawa today. Surely the requests of the department in Nova Scotia should be accepted.
I have not told the whole story, but private members from all parts of Canada should join forces with the hon. member from Davenport, so that we in Nova Scotia will not be "the forgotten part of Canada."
I do not want hon. members to think, even if we have not had fair treatment and even if we have not prospered as we should, that we have not great resources and great production, shipped away, it is true, mostly in the rough and unrefined form when industry should be based upon it at home. This was well pointed out by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Stanfield) in his splendid speech in this debate when he said:
Many Canadians who have never been to the maritimes seem to have the idea that maritimers are only heweTS of wood and drawers of water. This certainly is a mistaken idea. The maritimes are a beautiful country and the maritimers are the highest type of Canadian citizens.
Nova Scotia must indeed have great wealth as well as great thrift, or it would not have the capacity to purchase the long list of articles and commodities from central Canada

totalling many millions of dollars every year with a minimum of reciprocation. The heads of industry and bankers marvel at our purchases of motor cars, trucks, tires, batteries, farm machinery, cement, electric motors, tobacco, sugar, flour, radios, medicines, tools, jewellery and a hundred and one articles, and still we are able to educate our boys and girls so that they may be enticed away from home to take places at the top all over Canada. We are now told that there is to be a big increase in freight rates on our purchases and sales. We in the maritimes threw in our lot with Quebec and Ontario and, if they are to supply us with our necessities such as motor cars, trucks, cement, farm machinery, electric motors and such articles, I think we have the right to have them delivered to us freight paid at the lowest factory prices.
For better or for worse, we are part of Canada which has a proud place in the world today. Our people are more and more coming to the opinion that we have not had a fair deal. We in Nova Scotia want our proper place as an integral part of this great and expanding country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, consideration of a national budget raises the question of fundamental principles which govern in the national economy. To say that we cannot achieve national greatness unless we lay down and pursue sound long-range objectives and sound fundamental principles is to make an assertion which is selfevident. The point at issue, however, is what constitutes sound long-range objectives and sound fundamental principles. Each political party represented in this house considers that the fundamental principles and objectives to which it subscribes are sound, even though they are at variance with those of other parties. These principles therefore cannot all be right and neither can they all be wrong; and I doubt very much that it will ever be determined in this house which of these principles are sound and which are not. The political party atmosphere will not permit such to be done. "My party; right or wrong, my party," remains the dominant attitude of all political parties in this house. The most that can be hoped for is that the discussion and debate upon these issues in parliament will enable the electors to draw their own conclusions and determine their own course of action, and in the few moments at my disposal I wish to make my small contribution to that end.
So confused are the issues today that it is necessary that we define more carefully than ever before each and every term we use. There

The Budget-Mr. Kuhl
can be no intelligent discussion of any subject until we first define our terms. As simple as they are, such terms as "democracy," "freedom," "security" and so on, today mean different things to different people. That is equally true of many other terms we use such as "capitalism," "free enterprise", "private enterprise," "full employment," "socialism," "communism", and so forth. Such confusion is abroad today that we find totalitarianism masquerading under the cloak of democracy, slavery being represented as freedom and anti-Christianity being propagated under the sacred name of Christianity. How imperative therefore that we have a clear conception of what is involved in the terms which we use. I should like to use my time on this occasion to indicate my conception of some of the terms to which I have referred.
I wish, first of all, to indicate what conditions I think must prevail before our society can be characterized as a genuine democracy. As to definitions, I prefer the one given by Major C. H. Douglas, the founder of social credit principles, when he said that democracy is government in accordance with the will of the people. This means that in a genuine democracy the ^people should be able to get the results they want from the management of their affairs.
Accepting this as a general definition of democracy, I think it is fair to say that systems which have been designated as democratic have failed dismally to produce results in accordance with the will of the people. Even in countries where the outward forms of democracy have been most successfully established, the people have obtained very few of the results they wanted. On the contrary they have had insecurity, poverty, want and war meted out to them, and have seen individual freedom diminishing at an alarming rate. Instead of government in accordance with the will of the people, we have had government contrary to the will of the people.
The people of Canada are not getting from their present government the results which they desire. The people of Canada are willing and able to produce the things required for a standard of living very much higher than what they are at present enjoying. The standard of living which the people are entitled to enjoy should be limited only by their willingness to produce and their capacity to consume. At the present level of prices that should certainly represent an income of at least $4,000 a year, tax free, for every family of four. And as industry gets back to capacity production on a peacetime basis a substantial improvement on that amount should be possible.
I say, sir, that the people of Canada are willing and able to produce goods and services necessary to sustain and improve such a standard of living. But they can neither raise production completely to those levels, nor can they bring about the complete distribution of that production unless their efforts are accompanied by certain actions which the government must take, actions which the people themselves cannot take and which must therefore be undertaken by the government on their behalf.
The present government has not taken such steps and has not legislated in such a manner as to permit the people to produce to the limit of their desire to consume, and which will permit them to consume to the extent of that production. The present government is not governing in accordance with the will of the people of this country.
The question therefore arises: how can a government be compelled to govern in accordance with the will of the people? Before this question can properly be answered, another matter of fundamental importance must be determined, and that is the real purpose and function of parliament. Parliament today has departed a very great distance from its real purpose and function. I consider that Major Douglas has stated the purpose of parliamentary institutions as well as anyone has. In a speech at Buxton on June 9, 1934, he made the following statement:
Instead of electing representatives to inform hankers and industrialists (who understand the technique of their jobs perfectly) how to do them, and to pass a multitude of laws which, while providing unnecessary jobs for large numbers of people who could be better employed still further impede industry, the business of democracy is to elect representatives who will insist upon results and will if necessary pillory the actual individuals who are responsible either for the attainment of results or their non-attainment.
It is not a bit of use asking democracies to decide upon matters of technique; and it is quite certain, as has already been demonstrated, that if you throw a plan to a democracy it will be torn to shreds.
It is not the business of the parliamentary machine to reform, for instance, the financial system. It is the business of the parliamentary machine to transmit the desires of the people for results out of the financial system, and to transmit to the people the names of individuals who are responsible for the financial system, so that by the exercise of the right of eminent domain, which has undoubtedly been established as vested in the representatives of the people, they may if necessary take steps to remove those responsible for impeding the will of the people. If it is pleaded in extenuation that those in charge of any particular function of the state, such as finance, do not know how to produce the results desired, then it is the business of parliament to provide them with all the advice available. But if they will neither take action within a

The Budget-Mr. Kuhl

reasonable period of time and will not accept advice if provided, then it is the business of the representatives of the people to remove them, whether they are alleged to be operating under a system of private enterprise or as public departments.
In the fewest possible words Major Douglas contends that the chief duty of a member of parliament consists in seeing that the people get the results which they want from the management of their affairs, and not in suggesting the methods by which those results can be obtained.
In another part of his Buxton speech, Major Douglas makes the following comment upon the situation into which parliament has drifted as a consequence of concerning itself about methods instead of results:
We elect parliamentary representatives at the present time to pass laws of a highly technical nature, not to ensure that certain results are achieved. As a result of this, not merely in this country but everywhere in the world, as far as my observation takes me, we are witnessing a set of second-rate experts in the seats of government ineffectively endeavouring to give technical direction to a set of first-rate experts who are actually carrying on the functions by which society lives.
I agree whole-heartedly with these statements and I suggest it is imperative that Canadians take steps immediately to rehabilitate democracy in Canada in accordance with the principles suggested by Major Douglas. It is not the duty of members of parliament to pose as experts on methods. It is quite in order for a member of parliament to be an expert on methods, but it is not his function as a representative of the people. It is his business to see that the people get the results which they want. And if he is not an expert himself, it is his duty to see that experts are hired to devise methods by which results can be obtained.
Therefore, on behalf of the electors of Jasper-Edson, whose spokesman I am privileged to be, I demand that the government, and in particular the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) see that methods are devised which will permit the electors of Jasper-Edson, along with the rest of the people of Canada, to produce to the limit of their desire to consume, and which will permit them to buy to the extent of that production, without in any way interfering with their individual and personal freedom.
If the experts at present employed are either unable or unwilling to produce the results desired within a reasonable period of time, then the government should dismiss them and replace them with individuals who can and will produce results. I quite realize, however, that the voice of one member of parliatMr. Kuhl.]
ment, or of even a dozen, is not sufficient to compel the government to take action along these lines. Were a majority of members from both sides of the house to do so, I am satisfied that it would not be long before such results would be forthcoming. The reasons that a majority of members in this house will not rise and make such demands of the government are twofold: party politics and lack of organization on the part of the people, such that they can insist upon obedience to their *will. The political party system makes it very difficult for the people to exercise their democratic privileges and assume their personal responsibilities, even if they are so inclined. The political party system cannot properly serve democracy. Once every four or five years, the people are given an opportunity to vote simultaneously for a candidate and a party platform. The people as a whole have no voice in deciding the contents of these platforms. They are prepared by a small minority group with an eye to vote-catching. Often the platform deals for the most part with methods, concerning which neither the drafters of the platform nor the general public are qualified to form a wise judgment. Nothing could be more confusing. Elections find the voter wondering whether to vote for a candidate, a platform or a political party.

After the election, the successful candidates cannot be controlled by the electorate. They vote themselves their own indemnities and submit to the dictates of a few party "bosses" who are the party organization between elections. The policies which

The Budget-Mr. Kuhl
have been implemented under party government are certainly not in accordance with the will of the people.
Political parties need a considerable amount of money to maintain their organizations and their propaganda. Those who provide the party funds expect favours for their support. subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I grant that so long as there are political parties, no matter what name they assume, they are subject to the same abuses, although we hope that we have a cleaner record in our party than has been the case with some of the older parties.
Political parties divide the people into conflicting camps-each striving to win their support to vote them into office and each attempting to discredit the other parties. Under such a system no representative, however sincere, can possibly serve the interests of the people effectively. The party system makes this impossible. "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation", and if one may judge by the results of the political party system in every country, it has all but succeeded in achieving this. There is no reason or need for the people of Canada to be divided into a number of conflicting political camps, because all people want substantially the same results from the management of their affairs.
All people want and must have adequate food, clothing and shelter, even though their individual tastes in this respect may vary considerably.
All people want security in old age or when they suffer loss of income through illness, unemployment or other causes
All people want the personal and individual freedom to worship God according to the dictates of conscience; to choose or refuse to do whatever they wish, provided that in so doing they do not interfere with the same right of every other individual; to acquire by their honest efforts their fair share of the desirable things of life, such as education, property, luxuries and so forth.
The only difference of opinion which exists is regarding the methods by which these results can be obtained. However the people, as the supreme authority, should not be concerned with methods.
The concern which the people should have is for an organization through which they 83166-2104
can secure obedience to their will. Workers in industry, farmers and others, have found it necessary to organize as unions in order to gain the objective they want. Because the principle underlying trade union movements is right, they have had a measure of success in securing better working conditions and wages. Political and economic systems can be made to function in the best interests of the people, if they will organize for that purpose, just as trade unions organize for a more limited purpose.
It is gratifying to me to observe that such an organization has already commenced in Canada and that it is growing daily. The movement and the organization to which I refer is the Union of Electors. This movement is something new in the political life of Canada, but it is already far beyond the stage of infancy. Its greatest strength is at the moment in the province of Quebec, which is evident from the attention which the hon. members from the province of Quebec are paying to the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette), who was elected to this parliament, not as a member of a political party, but because of the assurance which he gave the electors of Pontiac that- he would at all times demand the results which they desired.
The Union of Electors is not a political party. It is a union of the voters who are organized to get the results desired in common by all the people, irrespective of race, religion or party affiliation.
The objectives of the Union of Electors are:
1.	To state the results wanted from the management of the affairs of the country in all spheres affecting the lives of the people.
2.	To control the elected representatives of the people at all times, and through them, all the people's governing bodies, local, provincial and national.
3.	To insist on and enforce obedience to the will of the people on all matters of policy.
It is only through such an organization of the electors that Canada or any other country can experience government in accordance with the will of the people. I am indeed glad, therefore, to see such an organization of the people developing in Canada, and I intend to do everything I can to encourage it and assist it until it encompasses the majority of Canadians from Vancouver to Halifax.
In my remarks thus far, Mr. Speaker, I have indicated some of the circumstances which I think must prevail in our society before it can be characterized as a genuine democracy. I have suggested that the duty of members of parliament in a democracy
The Budget-Mr. Kuhl

proper should be confined to securing results rather than devising and debating methods. I realize, however, that we shall not alter our course without a period of transition. Until the people are organized to demand otherwise, parliament will continue to discuss methods rather than results. Before concluding, therefore, I intend to contravene the principles which I have just enunciated, by making a few remarks concerning methods.
Judged from the point of view of orthodox budgets, this budget is no doubt as good a budget as any orthodox economist could draw up. My general criticism is that an orthodox budget does not reveal the true facts about the national economy. In a substantial measure, this budget falsifies and conceals the real economic facts and conditions of this country. I deplore this situation and, on behalf of the people who sent me here, I protest against it.
I say that this budget falsifies and conceals the real economic condition of the nation because it deals only with money which the government extracts from the taxpayers and indicates no relationship between the money in the hands of the people and the goods and services which they are expected to buy.
The question at the root of the whole situation is one of the monetization of real wealth. In the highly industrialized and power-mechanized system of production of today, a barter system of exchange is obviously impossible. The only means whereby the people can draw from the pool of national production is through the monetization of that pool of production. Money must be created and must be put into circulation before goods can be either produced or distributed. In a modem economy this is done largely through loans to industry created and lent by the chartered banks. The orthodox economist assumes that this means is sufficient to enable the people to buy back their production. He believes that the total money in the hands of the people is always equal to the total of the prices of goods which they are expected to buy. He believes that production and income are one and the same thing. Because he believes this, he concludes that if part of the national production is to be diverted to public services of various kinds, the only method of doing so is to take from the people in taxes an amount of money sufficient to divert to public service whatever part of the national production is required. Such a conclusion would be sound if the premise upon which it is based were sound. I contend, sir, that the premise is most unsound, and therefore any conclusion based upon it must also be unsound.

In normal times when there is not an abnormal expansion of capital goods, as during a war, and immediately following a war. income does not keep pace with production. Money income is always less than the price value of production. This premise is not conceded by orthodox economists, but it is nevertheless borne out by the facts of industry. Because money income is never equal to national production in normal times, I say it is unnecessary and unsound for a government, with control over the nation's money, to go into debt or to levy taxes in order to divert part of the national production to public services.
In normal times a country suffers from a lack of purchasing power as compared with its producing power. There is an actual physical shortage of money in the hands of all the people collectively as compared with the total prices of goods. An increasing proportion of our national production remains unmonetized. This unmonetized portion of national production has been partly monetized in the past by government borrowings of newly created bank money which is paid out for public works, bonuses, subsidies and for other governmental purposes. This does not balance the economy, however, for this money is charged to the national debt to be collected through taxes. But it is mathematically impossible for the people to buy the total of national production and pay these taxes as well. The most popular misconception as to why the poor are poor is that the rich are rich. Many imagine that their incomes are low because the incomes of others are too high. The implied remedy is, therefore, to tax the rich. I am not suggesting that the rich ought not to be taxed, but I do assert that it is impossible to distribute the whole of national production by taxing the money from the rich and giving it to the poor.

Up until the present budget the government has incurred huge deficits which have been met by government borrowings of newly created bank money. This freshly created bank money which was borrowed by the government was used to meet governmental expenditures including the payment of subsidies. It is true that these borrowings are charged to the national debt and are collectible through taxation, but the fact of the matter is that the debt is never collected; it is merely refunded, the principal remaining and the interest compounding.
It is therefore incorrect to say that subsidies have come out of taxation. They have come out of newly created bank money, which is borrowed by the government, but which is never collected in taxation.

speechtext:
In other words, part of the national production which could not be, and was not monetized through the usual routine of business, was monetized by the government through the use of debt money. I contend, sir, that if any part of the national production must be monetized by the government in order that the people as a whole can avail themselves of the total production of the nation, then that monetization must be brought about free of debt and free of taxation. This I consider to be one of the most important and most sacred duties of any modern government.
When the state, through its appropriate financial agency, issues debt-free, tax-free money in payment for public services, bonuses, subsidies, et cetera, it is not playing Santa Claus, and neither is the public getting something for nothing. When the government creates and pays out money in this manner, it is merely acting as the agent of all the people in monetizing goods which already exist, which have been produced by the people
and therefore belongs to them, but which they cannot acquire until such goods are represented by money.
Socialists contend that the state cannot distribute goods which it does not own. The fact that this is being done every day through family allowances, old age pensions and in many other ways, proves the fallacy of such a contention. When the government augments the regular incomes of the people with money sufficient to raise total income to where it is equal to total production, consumers can buy all goods offered for sale whether they are privately produced or publicly.
Had governments monetized the unmonetized portion of national production with debt-free and tax-free money in the past, there would be no national debt today and there would be no interest charges to be paid in the form of taxes. The national debt is a national lie. Canadians have always paid their way physically in anything they have ever done, whether it was the promotion of peacetime enterprise or the waging of war. The only costs in doing anything are physical costs, that is, human energy and physical materials. Canadians, collectively, have always met all physical costs. Then how can it be logically argued that a national debt is unavoidable?
The only reason that there is a national debt is that governments have not been faithful to their sacred trust. The highest and most sacred prerogative which the crown can enjoy is the exclusive monopoly of the creation and issue, in the original instance, of all the money of the nation. Successive governments in Canada have, by degrees, surrendered this most sacred prerogative into the hands of private persons.
As a consequence of this most dastardly betrayal, the whole nation is now in bondage to the mere handful of individuals who exercise this prerogative. Instead of these private persons proceeding to the crown for the use of sums of money, the government now goes cap in hand to these private purveyors of financial credit, and mortgages the entire nation to them.
This nefarious practice has now reached such proportions that the interest charges alone on the national debt are almost equivalent to the total governmental pre-war expenditure, and the end is nowhere in sight under the present financial policy.
I say, sir, that those who have been and who continue to be responsible for these reprehensible circumstances should be regarded as arch-criminals, who should be tried for their crimes and punished accordingly.
The Budget-Mr. Kuhl

In an earlier debate in this house, one of the C.C.P. members, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in disparaging tones suggested that the Social Credit members do not believe in anything except just printing a lot of money. Such a statement carries with it the implication that money in a modern economy is of very little consequence, and that very little attention need be paid to the manner in which it is created and put into circulation. Such a statement merely indicates how badly the hon. member for Cape Breton South and those who think as he does, are misinformed on the subject of money.
I readily grant that the things which make up a standard of living are the goods and services which the people are capable of producing and desirous of consuming, but the point which the hon. member for Cape Breton South seems to overlook is that the production and distribution of goods and services in a modern economy are absolutely impossible without the use of money. The starting point of every economic activity today is money. No matter how great the natural resources of the country may be, and no matter how willing and able the people may be to develop those resources, not a wheel in industry turns until money is first put into circulation.
Money is the mainspring in a modern economy, and without it the economy stops dead. Money is the master-key to the whole economic question. Hence those who enjoy the privilege of creating and issuing the money of the nation hold the power of life and death over the people of the nation by virtue of that privilege. Is it any wonder that one of the oldest bankers, Baron Rothschild, at one time said, "Permit me to create the money of a nation and I care not who makes its laws"?
The private bankers today are the sole arbiters in Canada as to how much money goes into circulation, as to where it goes into circulation and as to the terms under which it goes into circulation. This places governments and the people entirely at the mercy of the private bankers of this country. It is positively idle, therefore, to suggest that money is of very little consequence in a modern economy.
What is the problem of the old age pensioners? It is purely a money problem. Those who ask for more generous pensions take it for granted, and' rightly so, that goods and services are available in sufficient quantities to maintain them in decency and health. But all that they are lacking is money with which to acquire the goods and services which are available in abundance.
What is the problem of the blind and the otherwise incapacitated? It is nothing but a

lack of money with which to buy the goods and services which are available in abundance. What is the problem of the farmers and other primary producers? It is nothing other than money which must be paid out in the form of subsidies and bonuses in order to guarantee them their proper proportion of the national income.
Almost every individual in the nation considers that his income is too low and that his taxes are too high. In other words, he is lacking in money. And so one could go through the entire economy and find that the problem in almost every case is a lack of money. It is taken for granted, and rightly so, that the goods and services are available, or will be before long, to support the higher incomes which are demanded.
However the only source of money which the government chooses to use to attempt to augment the incomes of the people is nothing but debt and taxation, both of which aggravate the situation instead of improving it.
The Progressive Conservative members deserve the criticism which they receive for advocating increased services and decreased expenditures in one and the same breath; for, were they in the seats of the present government, their source of money would also be nothing other than debt and taxation. They plead, of course, that they would eliminate extravagant expenditures; but, even were they to do so, the amount of money which would be secured by that means would be a mere bagatelle, as compared with what is required to bring about a balanced economy.
The C.C.F. members seem to suggest that they advocate sources of money other than taxation, but a close analysis of their statements indicates that their proposals for raising money for governmental purposes involve nothing other than taxation and are therefore no different from the proposals of the Liberals and the Progressive Conservatives.
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), in the debate upon the subsidy question, stated that the money for subsidies under a C.C.F. administration would come out of increased production. Such a statement may seem to mean something else, but it cannot mean anything other than that the money would be derived from taxation, for, regardless of by how much production is increased, all other economic factors are increased proportionately. If national production is doubled, the deficiency between income and production is also doubled, and no scheme of taxation can ever bring about the complete distribution of national production. The C.C.F. proposals are therefore just as inef-

The Budget-Mr. C. T. Richard
fective as are those of the two old parties; in fact, they are exactly the same kind of proposals.
Therefore, inasmuch as all our major national problems resolve themselves into the one problem of an insufficiency of money, I contend that the system of debt and taxation must be completely abolished except for the purpose of redistributing part of the national income, if such is deemed necessary, and for the purpose of withdrawing excess credits if such a situation should ever arise. All funds required by the government for the purpose of monetizing the unmonetized portion of national production must be provided by the government through its own financial agency, debt-free and tax-free.
The rectification of this one fundamental feature of our national economy is the key to the solution of all our problems. The nationalization or socialization of any part or of all of industry and finance, whether monopoly controlled or not, is as unnecessary as it is undesirable, to bring about a complete and equitable distribution of national production.
The people of Canada, on their individual initiative as responsible private enterprisers, are willing and able to produce all that they will ever desire to consume. So long as the government, as the agent of the people, sees to it that the entire production of the nation is monetized so that it can be distributed in its entirety, I am prepared to depend upon the people working privately upon their own initiative to raise the production of the country to any desirable level whatsoever.
With sufficient money in their hands at all times to buy their fair share of national production, economic security with individual and personal freedom becomes a reality for each and every Canadian.
In a world of confusion, the people of Canada have a better opportunity than those of any other country in the world to assert themselves as the supreme authority in the land and so establish a genuine democracy that will ensure a high standard of living with the freedom to enjoy it. Thus Canada may demonstrate to the world that the causes of economic disaster, aggression ^nd war, which exist in the organization of society, may be removed by the people themselves. This is the challenge which faces the people of Canada today. They may apathetically drift along the course now leading us to disaster, or they may lead the world toward that genuine Christian democracy which will enable all nations to live at peace with one another.

speechtext:
-particularly from your extreme left. As to the particulars of the budget, I intend to say very little. I should like, however, to be permitted to make a few remarks in a general way on the situation of the maritime provinces. I believe this situation is a subject which is quite relevant to the one we are discussing at the present time.
If no real criticism has come from the other side of the house or even from the press of the country I believe it is due to the fact that our opponents and our critics have been taken by surprise and that in the matter of concessions in taxation the budget disclosed much more than they anticipated. Indeed, prior to the presentation of the budget there was such a pressure brought upon this government and upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to wipe out all controls and to make sweeping reductions in taxation that, after hearing the Minister of Finance, we may say of him that he is bold when being cautious and even cautious when he is bold.
I share the opinion, however, with some other members of the house that perhaps the Minister of Finance could have shown a smaller surplus by extending certain services or else by reducing taxation along some lines. But we on this side of the house-knowing the Minister of Finance as we do, as a true Liberal-know that he has the interests of the people at heart and that, should an emergency arise, he will certainly make good use of that surplus.
I believe that we can say that this budget, although not the first one since the cessation of hostilities, may be called the first peacetime budget, for it has all the earmarks of peacetime economy. We have had several budgets since hostilities ceased, but there were such extraordinary expenditures to be made, such as those for bringing from overseas all our troops, rehabilitation, replacing those soldiers in their former positions, maintaining a large personnel and many other matters arising out of the war that it was necessary to maintain a high rate of taxation. This budget we find is quite commensurate to our needs and quite within our means.
The Budget-Mr. C. T. Richard

We may, therefore, call it a peacetime budget, for we find alleviation in the matter of taxation and we find that we are again getting into our normal way of life. We are, therefore, charting our course to a permanent peacetime economy, which must be planned on a firm basis, which must be planned shrewdly, which must contain policies which, projected. into the future, will ensure that, whatever happens outside our own boundaries, we shall not strike shoals which may be dangerous to our own domestic economy. We must adopt policies whereby every province and every section of the country will derive equal advantages. We fashion policies whereby no province will benefit at the expense of another and no one section will expand industrially while another section languishes. I believe that we have not followed that course in the past. I believe that we have adopted policies-both fiscal, tariff and otherwise-whereby industry has been centralized in just two provinces in this dominion, and naturally so has capital, to the great detriment of the other provinces, particularly our own maritime provinces.
I crave the indulgence of the house to be allowed to speak for a few moments about conditions in the maritimes along the lines which I have just mentioned. I know that hon. members, after hearing members from the maritimes, may think that we are provincial, and that we are forever bewailing our lot; but I want to remind hon. member*1' that we feel we have grievances which are real; and until a solution of these problems is found, I say that we shall not have a true economy in this country.
You often hear it said that in the maritime provinces we discuss parting or separating from confederation. It may be true that perhaps at times we regret that we ever entered confederation; but I want to assure the house that it is my belief that at no time was public opinion ever crystallized to the point where any decision was arrived at to take that step. . We cannot understand, however, how the rest of Canada cannot see that we have grievances, that we have not shared equally with the other provinces in the advantages accruing from confederation, and that no real effort has been made to see what caused that result and whether this down trend in our economic life cannot be stopped.
It is true that we have appointed commissions to study conditions in the maritimes, and I may mention two particularly: the Duncan royal commission, and the White commission. I might also mention the Rowell-Sirois commission which embraced conditions

in the maritimes. I now wish to refer to these commissions for one particular purpose, and that is to show that those commissions came to the decision which I desire to point out here. I wish to read just one paragraph from the Duncan royal commission report to show how it proves our case. This quotation from the Duncan commission report is found at page 20 of the report of the White commission:
We are far from saying that the dominion, within its sphere of control, has done all for the maritime provinces which it should have done.
It then goes on to quote how Canada, a
vast country, had to look after new provinces and was preoccupied in other business, as it were, and how possibly the maritimes- the old provinces-were neglected. Then the conclusion of that paragraph is as follows:
But reasonable balance is within accomplishment if there be periodic stocktaking.
That is the suggestion made by the DuncaD commission.
In support of my claim that we did not derive all the benefits which should have accrued from confederation to the maritime provinces, I read from the White commission report at page 20:
We are in accord with the claim of the maritime provinces and with the finding of the Duncan commission that these provinces have not shared proportionately with the other provinces of Canada in the economic advantages accruing to the dominion as a whole from confederation and in our recommendations have *taken it into account as one of the most impressive elements in their case for more favourable financial arrangements.
The recommendations of those two commissions were carried into effect in so far as financial arrangements are concerned. Increased subsidies were granted. Freight rates were cut down. But I submit that these were only palliatives which never did settle firmly and finally the problems of the maritimes, and it was never the intention to settle them by these recommendations.
There are those who contend that the situation in the maritimes would have arisen notwithstanding confederation, and that these conditions were bound to come. I do not quite share this opinion. I believe that our situation today is due to confederation, to the relinquishment of the rights which we then possessed and the granting to the central power of responsibility for policies, the exercise of which brought about the conditions in the maritimes today. It is not pleasant perhaps to go back to conditions existing several generations ago. However, probably it is necessary to do so in order to ascertain what caused the economic situation that exists in

The Budget-Mr. C. T. Richard
the maritimes today. Sometimes these things are not brought about by one event but by a chain of events which culminate in a situation which has not been foreseen.
Let me take you back, sir, to the days of confederation. We in the maritimes were prosperous; we were the most prosperous section of British North America. We were masters of our own customs and excise; we held the gateways through which would flow our foreign trade both export and import. We knew the progress that had been made in the country to the south, how they had developed their ports on the Atlantic seaboard. We could visualize, therefore, that our own future would be patterned along the same line and that we would reach the same prosperous condition they enjoyed. When we entered confederation, therefore, we knew we were jeopardizing a great deal. So it is not surprising that when confederation was first discussed in the maritimes the leaders of industry at that time did not entirely agree with it, because they knew just what it would mean to jeopardize the advantages we then possessed. However, confederation was put forward for the purpose of uniting the provinces into an economic unit, as well as for military purposes. That induced the leaders of the maritimes to enter into the pact, for it became quite evident that the provinces needed an outlet to the sea; that some day they might be attacked, and the St. Lawrence route alone was not sufficient to ensure their defence.
Therefore we -went into confederation. When we compare our position at the time of confederation with our position today; when we view the progress that has been made in the country to the south, the development of their great ports of Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Portland; when we realize that we have the same geographical position and the same energetic people, with only an imaginary line separating us-when we consider all these things we wonder why, from an economic point of view, we have remained at a standstill and progress has passed us by.
I have shown that no personal motives induced us to enter confederation. The sole aim of the maritimers was to build a strong nation, and I may say the attitude of the maritimers has not changed one iota since that time. We have supported every move and every expenditure that have been made to develop this into a great country. We contributed to the development of the west, even though hon. members from that part of the country may not see it in that way. We assisted in a costly immigration policy from 1900 on, though we could see we had not the
advantages possessed by the west and that, therefore, we would derive very little benefit from such a policy. Our railways having been built practically at the expense of the public treasury, we contributed our share to the construction of the railway systems of this dominion. We encouraged the development of the inland water route by the construction of canals between our lakes and by the deepening of the St. Lawrence river in order to make Montreal one of the greatest ports in the world, even though we knew it was to our own detriment. In every way the provinces aimed first to make of this a great country, notwithstanding the fact that sometimes it might have been detrimental to the best interests of the maritimes themselves.
Need I cite any more examples to show our -unselfishness in the history of our country since confederation? May I point out again that when the subject of a rapprochement between the provinces and Ottawa was discussed, the maritimes were the first to come forward and offer their cooperation; and here today we are relinquishing certain rights to the dominion government, though again this is to our detriment, because these money grants, being based on population, will not bring the same benefit to us since our population will not increase in the same ratio as that of the other provinces. Again we have worked against our own interests and for the benefit of Canada, to make it a great country. I am sorry that up to the present these conferences have not been successful. The whole problem as I have seen it-because as a member of the New Brunswick government prior to the last war I attended two of these conferences-is the suspicion and distrust the provinces feel for the central authorities in Ottawa; and until that distrust is banished from their minds there will not be a successful conclusion to these conferences.
I would not speak about these maritime matters at such length if the other evening the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nieol) had not made certain suggestions to improve our economic conditions. I wish to thank him for what he said and for the support he has given us, and if I answer him I want to assure the hon. gentleman that I do so in a friendly way. He told us that to improve the economic position of the maritimes it would be necessary to develop Grand Falls to the full' extent. I want to tell him that prior to 1925 the Liberal government of New Brunswick had all plans prepared for that development, but the Conservative party came into power and turned everything over to the International Paper Company. that day forward the province of New Brunswick lost control of Grand Falls. Then he also advocated construction of the Chignecto canal. I want to say that we approve the stand he has taken, that everyone from the maritimes stands behind this project. I believe it would bring to the maritime provinces the New England markets, which are the natural markets for the maritimes since they are closer to our shores. We cannot expect the upper provinces to be the sole markets for our exportable surplus in sea, forest or farm products. In my estimation the New England states are our natural markets, as they were before, confederation.
A moment ago, Mr. Speaker, I told you how Grand Falls was lost to the province of New Brunswick by being turned over lock, stock and barrel to the International Paper Company, that octopus in the power and paper field. That was one occasion when we were sold down the river, but I will tell you of another. In 1911, when the question of the approval of the trade treaty between the United States and Canada came before the Canadian people, by flag waving and the slogan, "No truck nor trade with the Yankees", we were hoodwinked into refusing that approval, something we have regretted ever since. That was another occasion when we were sold down the river.

speechtext:
By the Conservative party that come into power, controlled by the industralists of central Canada who made us believe that they had a ready market for all we could produce, but who today too often consider us as their poor cousins.
Since my time is limited, I should now to say a few words about something which is peculiar to the maritime provinces, and which means a great deal to them. I refer to the fishing industry. Only a few days ago I came across some figures which showed that the production of sea products from the maritime provinces has been valued at 831 million, and this figure does not include the processed value, which is considerable.
This administration has done wonderful things for the fisheries. It is the first administration which has ever really helped the fishermen by giving them assistance in the construction of their boats, in the establishing of processing plants and freezing plants, and in the securing of new markets. Today in the person of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) we have a man who does not waste his time or the time of the house in saying what he proposes to do, but rather goes ahead and does things. I am sure every member from the maritime provinces will stand back of him in that. However the fishermen in the maritimes need better facilities.
Before concluding, let me say that I blame no political party, and no particular regime for our situation. Sometimes I admit that we are partly to blame ourselves. Our whole economic future depends upon the establishment and the promulgation of certain policies by the central government, and by the financial institutions over which we have no control, except indirectly.
We of the maritimes do not ask for any special privileges or hand-outs; rather, we wish to share in the progress of the country. We are convinced that Canada cannot be a great nation if one section of it is economically weak. The strength of confederation may be likened to a chain which is as strong as its weakest link. We therefore urge our administration and our financial institutions, all those who are interested in making this a great nation, to study our problems. We ask every maritimer-because there are some to be found from coast to coast-to become good will ambassadors on our behalf, and to preach what we have been attempting to show the country. When I say that there are mari-timers from coast to coast I mean that, because of economic conditions, they have been forced to leave our provinces and have established themselves successfully in all parts of Canada. At one time, indeed if not today, the heads of four of the biggest banking institutions of Canada were maritimers.
Maritimers are maritimers always. They cannot forget the land of their birth, that land whose beauty in its rivers, its lakes, its mountains and its seashore is unexcelled anywhere. But those maritimers are also Canadians at heart. While they may be maritimers by attachment, they are Canadians first and always. Perhaps their feelings are best expressed in the words of that maritime poet who said:
Friends I have found in far and alien places;
Beauty and ardour in unfamiliar faces.
But deep in my heart is the land I call home,
Canadian am I in blood and bone.
